items.title: Figure 14 caption question: A student heats 0.250 kg of an unknown liquid on a hot plate and plots temperature against time. (a) Explain why the hot plate must deliver thermal energy at a constant rate in order to find the liquid's specific heat from the graph. (b) The plate delivers 180 W (180 J each second) and the straight part of the graph rises at 0.30 K/s. Find the specific heat.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.250 kg, power 𝑃= 180 J/s, slope 𝛥𝑇/ 𝑡= 0.30 K/s. Find 𝐶.
Specific heat is 𝐶= 𝑄/ (𝑚𝛥𝑇). On a temperature-versus-time graph we know 𝛥𝑇 and the time, not 𝑄 directly. If the source delivers power 𝑃 steadily, then 𝑄= 𝑃𝑡.

(a) Substituting 𝑄= 𝑃𝑡 gives 𝛥𝑇/ 𝑡= 𝑃/ (𝑚𝐶). The slope of the graph is therefore a single number, 𝑃/ (𝑚𝐶), only if 𝑃 is constant. If the power changed, the slope would change for reasons unrelated to the liquid's specific heat, and 𝑄 could not be found from the elapsed time. (b) Solve the slope relation for 𝐶: 𝐶=

answer.html: (a) With a constant heating rate the energy added is proportional to time (𝑄= 𝑃𝑡), so the slope is proportional to 1 / 𝐶 and can be converted into a specific heat. (b) 𝐶= 2.4 × 10<sup>3</sup> J/(kg · K).

check.html: The value is close to that of methanol (2450), a sensible number for a liquid, and it is lower than water's, so the liquid would heat faster than water under the same plate.

items.title: 19: How much thermal energy is needed to change 0.250 kg of ice at −25.0°C into water at 0.0°C?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.250 kg, 𝐶<sub>𝑖𝑐𝑒</sub>= 2060 J/(kg · K), 𝐻<sub>𝑓</sub>= 3.34 × 10<sup>5</sup> J/kg, 𝛥𝑇= 25.0 K. Find total 𝑄.
Two steps: warm the ice to its melting point (𝑄= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇), then melt it at constant temperature (𝑄= 𝑚𝐻<sub>𝑓</sub>).

check.html: Melting dominates (about 6.5 times the warming step), which is typical for ice.

items.title: 20: How much thermal energy is needed to change 0.150 kg of water at 45.0°C into water vapor at 125.0°C?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.150 kg; 𝐶<sub>𝑤𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟</sub>= 4180, 𝐶<sub>𝑣𝑎𝑝𝑜𝑟</sub>= 2020 J/(kg · K); 𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg.
Three steps: warm the liquid from 45.0°C to 100.0°C, vaporize at 100.0°C, then warm the vapor to 125.0°C.

check.html: Vaporization is about 89% of the total, consistent with the long flat segment on a heating curve at the boiling point.

answer.html: 𝐻<sub>𝑓</sub>= 3.6 × 10<sup>4</sup> J/kg and 𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 5.3 × 10<sup>5</sup> J/kg (5.32 × 10⁵ before rounding).

items.title: 23 (Challenge): How much thermal energy is needed to change 0.150 kg of ice at −18.0°C into water vapor at 115.0°C?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.150 kg; 𝐶<sub>𝑖𝑐𝑒</sub>= 2060, 𝐶<sub>𝑤𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟</sub>= 4180, 𝐶<sub>𝑣𝑎𝑝𝑜𝑟</sub>= 2020 J/(kg · K); 𝐻<sub>𝑓</sub>= 3.34 × 10<sup>5</sup>, 𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg.
Five steps: warm ice to 0°C, melt, warm water to 100°C, vaporize, warm vapor to 115.0°C.

check.html: Vaporization (73% of the total) dominates, as it does on any heating curve for water where the boiling segment is the longest.

items.title: 24: A gas in a cylinder with a movable piston absorbs 220 J of heat from a burner and does 150 J of work pushing the piston outward. What is the change in the gas's thermal energy, and does its temperature rise or fall?

body.html: 𝑄= + 220 J (absorbed), 𝑊= 150 J (done by the gas). Find 𝛥𝑈.
First law: 𝛥𝑈= 𝑄−𝑊, where 𝑊 is the work done by the system. Thermal energy depends on temperature, so the sign of 𝛥𝑈 tells us whether the temperature rises.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑈= + 70 J; the thermal energy increases, so the gas's temperature rises.

check.html: The gas gained 220 J and gave away 150 J as work, leaving 70 J to warm it, so energy is conserved.

items.title: 25: A power sander does work on a 0.65 kg iron plate and warms it by 8.0°C. How much work did the sander do? (Assume no heat flows in or out.)

body.html: 𝑚= 0.65 kg, 𝐶= 450 J/(kg · K), 𝛥𝑇= 8.0 K. Assume no heat flows in or out (𝑄= 0).
First law: 𝛥𝑈= 𝑄−𝑊<sub>𝑏𝑦𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑒</sub>. With 𝑄= 0, 𝛥𝑈= −𝑊<sub>𝑏𝑦𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑒</sub>= 𝑊<sub>𝑜𝑛𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑒</sub>, so the work done by the sander on the plate equals the increase in thermal energy, 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇.

answer.html: 𝑊= 2.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> J done by the sander on the iron

check.html: About 2.3 kJ for a few degrees in a small metal plate is reasonable; positive because the sander adds energy.

items.title: 26: A 0.75 kg bag of lead shot is dropped from a height of 1.8 m onto the floor again and again. How many drops are needed to warm the shot by 2.0°C? (Assume all the energy of each drop becomes thermal energy of the shot.)

body.html: 𝑚= 0.75 kg, ℎ= 1.8 m, 𝐶<sub>𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑑</sub>= 130 J/(kg · K), 𝛥𝑇= 2.0 K, 𝑔= 9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>. Find the number of drops 𝑛.
Each drop converts 𝑚𝑔ℎ of gravitational potential energy to thermal energy when the bag hits. Needed thermal energy is 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇.
The mass cancels. A whole number of drops is needed, so round up.

answer.html: About 15 drops (𝑛= 14.7)

check.html: Each drop supplies 𝑚𝑔ℎ= 13 J, and 2.0 K needs 195 J, so 195 / 13.2 ≈15.

items.title: 27: Each stroke of a spoon stirring coffee does 0.040 J of work on the liquid. How many strokes would it take to warm 0.25 kg of coffee by 1.5°C (treat coffee as water)?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.25 kg, 𝐶= 4180 J/(kg · K), 𝛥𝑇= 1.5 K, 𝑊<sub>𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ</sub>= 0.040 J.
Work done on the coffee becomes thermal energy: 𝑛𝑊<sub>𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ</sub>= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇.

answer.html: About 3.9 × 10<sup>4</sup> strokes (39,000)

check.html: A huge number, which is why stirring never noticeably warms a drink.

check.html: Vaporization makes up 96% of the total, so the result is close to 𝑚𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 3.39 × 10<sup>5</sup> J.

items.title: Get It? (energy converted to a less useful form): Give an example, other than braking a car or a phone charger, of mechanical or electrical energy being converted to a less useful form.

body.html: Energy is conserved but spreads out as thermal energy, which is hard to reuse.
A superball dropped on the floor bounces lower each time, and its mechanical energy is gradually converted to thermal energy in the ball, floor and air. Rubbing your hands together warms them.

answer.html: Example: a bouncing superball. Its kinetic and potential energy turn into thermal energy in the ball, floor and air, which spreads out and cannot be used to make the ball bounce again.

check.html: In each example the final thermal energy is spread over many particles at a slightly higher temperature.

items.title: Get It? (uncontrolled system): A can of cold soda is left on the dashboard of a parked car on a hot day. Why is it an uncontrolled system, and what happens to its thermal energy?

body.html: An uncontrolled system has no outside agent keeping energy concentrated or kept out; energy follows the second law.

Nothing insulates or refrigerates the can. The car's air and dashboard are hotter, so their particles have a higher average kinetic energy than the can's. Collisions at the surface pass energy into the can. This continues until the can and its surroundings have the same average kinetic energy.

answer.html: No refrigerator or insulation controls the can, so thermal energy spontaneously flows from the hot car interior into the cooler can until both are at the same temperature, spreading the energy more evenly.

check.html: The reverse (the can getting colder while the car heats up) would need an outside agent doing work, like a refrigerator.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Systems and System Models: Describe a system model for a baked potato cooling on a plate after it leaves the oven, naming the system, boundary, inputs and outputs.

body.html: A system model names what is included, where the boundary is, and what crosses it.

Choose the system as the potato. The boundary is the potato's skin. Input: essentially none once it is out of the oven. Outputs: thermal energy leaving through the boundary by conduction to the plate, convection by air currents, radiation (infrared), and a little energy carried off by evaporating steam.

answer.html: System: the potato. Boundary: its skin. Input: none after leaving the oven. Outputs: thermal energy lost by conduction, convection, radiation and evaporation until the potato reaches room temperature.

check.html: If you widen the system to include the potato, plate and room, the transfers become internal and total energy is constant.

items.title: Get It? (second law with entropy): Use entropy to explain why a cup of hot tea never spontaneously gets hotter by taking energy from the cooler room.

body.html: Entropy measures energy dispersal; in natural processes, total entropy does not decrease.

Tea gaining energy from the cooler room would concentrate energy into a smaller region, lowering the total entropy of tea plus room. The reverse (tea losing energy to the room) spreads the energy out and raises entropy.

answer.html: The tea cools, rather than heats, because natural processes go in the direction that increases (or keeps constant) the total entropy; tea warming itself at the room's expense would decrease entropy, which does not happen without outside work.

check.html: This is the same reason a refrigerator needs a power cord: pushing energy from cold to hot takes work.

answer.html: 1: 29 J/K; 2: 35 J/K; 3: 1.9 J/K; 4: 17 J/K. Why they differ: (2) is bigger than (1) because it has more water, so it needs more heat (1.5 times as much), even though it is hotter, which lowers 𝛥𝑆 slightly. (3) is small because copper has a much smaller specific heat than water, so the same temperature step needs less heat. (4) melting needs far more heat than a 1 K rise in a small lead sample, so it produces a large entropy increase even at a high temperature.

check.html: All 𝛥𝑆 values are positive because energy was added to each system, and units are J/K.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Lesson 2 Problem 29: A car engine takes in 3000 J of thermal energy from burning fuel in one cycle and does 900 J of work. (a) Describe the energy transformations in the engine. (b) How much waste heat is expelled each cycle? (c) What happens to entropy?

body.html: 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub>= 3000 J, 𝑊= 900 J. Find 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub>.
A heat engine takes in heat 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub> from a hot source, converts part to work 𝑊, and expels waste heat 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> to a cold sink: 𝑊= 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub>−𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> (since 𝛥𝑈= 0 over a cycle).
Solve for the waste heat:

Thermal energy moves from the hot combustion gases into the engine, where part is transformed into mechanical energy (work), and the rest leaves as waste heat to the cooler surroundings (exhaust, radiator). The waste heat disperses thermal energy into the large, cooler surroundings, so energy is spread out more than before, which is an increase in entropy; no engine can avoid this.

answer.html: (a) Heat from burning fuel becomes work plus waste heat. (b) 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub>= 2100 J per cycle. (c) Entropy increases because the waste heat spreads thermal energy into the surroundings.

check.html: Energy in (3000 J) equals work out plus waste heat (900 + 2100), so the first law holds.

items.title: 30: Many old buildings are heated by steam radiators. (a) Explain how steam delivers heat to a room. (b) How much thermal energy is released when 0.80 kg of steam at 100°C condenses to water at 100°C in the radiator?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.80 kg, 𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg. Find 𝑄.
Condensation releases the heat of vaporization: 𝑄= −𝑚𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub> (the vapor loses 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg).

(a) Steam reaches the cooler radiator and condenses to liquid water. The energy that was absorbed when the water vaporized is given back, a large amount per kilogram. This energy is conducted through the radiator metal to the room air, and convection circulates the warm air around the room. (b) The thermal energy released by the steam: 𝑄= −𝑚𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= −(0.80 kg)(2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg) = −1.8 × 10<sup>6</sup> J

answer.html: (a) As the vapor condenses in the radiator it releases its heat of vaporization, which passes through the metal and warms the room air. (b) 1.8 × 10<sup>6</sup> J is released (negative 𝑄 for the steam).

check.html: The sign of 𝑄 for the steam is negative (it loses energy) and positive for the room.

check.html: Vaporization is about 89% of the total.

items.title: 33: A 180 kg forge hammer moving at 6.0 m/s strikes a 1.5 kg block of iron resting on an anvil and stops. The iron warms by 2.0°C. Explain where the hammer's energy goes, and find what fraction of it warmed the iron.

body.html: 𝑚<sub>ℎ</sub>= 180 kg, 𝑣= 6.0 m/s, 𝑚<sub>𝐹</sub><sub>𝑒</sub>= 1.5 kg, 𝐶<sub>𝑖𝑟𝑜𝑛</sub>= 450 J/(kg · K), 𝛥𝑇= 2.0 K.
Mechanical energy is converted into thermal energy in an inelastic collision (work done on the iron).
The hammer's kinetic energy is
The iron's thermal energy rises by
The fraction is
so about 42% of the hammer's energy ended up in the iron; the rest went into the anvil, hammer and surroundings as thermal energy and sound.

answer.html: When the hammer stops, its kinetic energy (3.2 × 10<sup>3</sup> J) is converted by the collision into thermal energy of the iron, anvil, hammer and air. About 1.4 × 10<sup>3</sup> J (42%) warmed the iron by 2.0°C; energy is conserved overall.

check.html: The iron's 1.35 × 10<sup>3</sup> J is less than the hammer's 3.2 × 10<sup>3</sup> J, as required.

items.title: 34: A scientist measures the temperature of the water at the top and at the bottom of a 90 m waterfall using very sensitive thermometers. Predict how the two readings compare, and explain.

body.html: Falling water loses gravitational potential energy; when it hits the bottom and churns, its kinetic energy becomes thermal energy.
Energy is conserved: the mechanical energy lost by the water (𝑚𝑔ℎ) appears as thermal energy, so the water at the bottom should be slightly warmer than at the top.

answer.html: The water at the bottom should read slightly warmer, because the potential energy the water loses in falling is converted into thermal energy when it crashes into the pool.

check.html: This is the first law applied to mechanical energy (work equals heat equivalent). The change is tiny, so sensitive thermometers are needed.

items.title: 35: A waterfall drops 82.0 m. Assuming all the gravitational potential energy lost becomes thermal energy of the water, how much warmer is the water at the bottom than at the top?

body.html: ℎ= 82.0 m, 𝑔= 9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 𝐶= 4180 J/(kg · K). Find 𝛥𝑇.
All potential energy becomes thermal energy: 𝑚𝑔ℎ= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇. The mass cancels.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑇= 0.192 K (0.192°C warmer at the bottom)

check.html: A fraction of a degree, which is why a very sensitive thermometer is needed to notice it.

items.title: 36: Explain, using entropy, what happens to energy when a wood stove is used to heat a cabin.

body.html: Entropy measures energy dispersal; it increases when energy spreads out.

Burning wood converts the concentrated chemical energy in the wood into thermal energy of the hot gases and the stove, then spreads it into the air in the cabin (and through the walls to the outdoors). The same energy is now spread over many more particles at a lower temperature, so it is much less available to do useful work.

answer.html: Burning wood takes energy concentrated in chemical bonds and disperses it as thermal energy among a huge number of air molecules (and out to the surroundings). Energy is more spread out, so entropy increases.

check.html: The total energy is conserved, but it can no longer be easily gathered back.

items.title: 37 (Critical Thinking): An evaporative cooler ("swamp cooler") blows air through wet pads in a dry climate and the air coming out is noticeably cooler. Explain why.

body.html: Evaporation needs the heat of vaporization (𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg for water).

Water in the pads evaporates quickly into the dry air. The energy to turn liquid into vapor comes from the surrounding air, so the air loses thermal energy and its temperature drops. The cooled air is blown into the room.

answer.html: As water in the pads evaporates, it absorbs a large amount of thermal energy (the heat of vaporization) from the passing air, which cools the air.

check.html: Same reason sweat cools you.

items.title: 3D Thinking: Model the operation of a steam engine (boiler, piston and condenser) and show where energy enters, is converted to work, and leaves.

body.html: A steam engine is a heat engine: 𝑊= 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub>−𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub>.

A simple 2D model, drawn as four panels of a boiler, piston and condenser: Stage Component What happens 1. Heating boiler fuel burns; water absorbs 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub> and boils to high-pressure steam 2. Expansion piston/cylinder steam pushes the piston and does work 𝑊 on the crankshaft; the steam cools 3. Exhaust condenser the used steam gives up waste heat 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> to cooling water or air and condenses 4. Return pump liquid water is pumped back to the boiler to repeat the cycle

answer.html: This is a hands-on model project, so no unique numerical answer exists (sample/expected response). A correct model shows the four stages above, labels 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub> (heat from burning fuel into the boiler), 𝑊 (work to the crankshaft) and 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> (waste heat released in the condenser), and notes that some energy is always lost to the surroundings.

check.html: Every model should show that 𝑊= 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub>−𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> with 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub>> 0.

items.title: Figure 14 caption question, why must energy be added at a constant rate?

body.html: Specific heat is 𝐶= 𝑄/ (𝑚𝛥𝑇). On a temperature-versus-time graph we know 𝛥𝑇 and the time, not 𝑄 directly.

If the source delivers power 𝑃 (joules per second), then 𝑄= 𝑃𝑡, and so 𝛥𝑇/ 𝑡= 𝑃/ (𝑚𝐶). The slope of the graph is therefore 𝑃/ (𝑚𝐶), a single number only if 𝑃 is constant. If the power changed, the slope would change for reasons unrelated to the water's specific heat, and 𝑄 could not be found from the elapsed time.

answer.html: With a constant heating rate the energy added is proportional to time (𝑄= 𝑃𝑡), so the slope of the curve is proportional to 1 / 𝐶. Only then can the slope be converted to a specific heat.

check.html: The nearly straight, steady rise between about 300 s and 800 s in Figure 14 shows constant heating.

items.title: 23 (Challenge), Ice at −30.0°C to vapor at 130.0°C

body.html: 𝑚= 0.300 kg; 𝐶<sub>𝑖𝑐𝑒</sub>= 2060, 𝐶<sub>𝑤𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟</sub>= 4180, 𝐶<sub>𝑣𝑎𝑝𝑜𝑟</sub>= 2020 J/(kg · K); 𝐻<sub>𝑓</sub>= 3.34 × 10<sup>5</sup>, 𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg.
Five steps: warm ice to 0°C, melt, warm water to 100°C, vaporize, warm vapor to 130.0°C.

check.html: Vaporization (72% of the total) dominates, as in Figure 12 where the D-to-E segment is the longest.

items.title: 24, Gas balloon absorbs 75 J but stays at the same temperature

body.html: 𝑄= + 75 J; temperature unchanged, so 𝛥𝑈= 0 (the thermal energy depends on temperature). Find 𝑊 done by the balloon.
First law: 𝛥𝑈= 𝑄−𝑊.

answer.html: 𝑊= 75 J (done by the balloon as it expands)

check.html: All the heat absorbed went into expansion work, none into raising the temperature.

items.title: 25, Drill heating an aluminum block

question.html: A drill heats a 0.40 kg aluminum block by 5.0°C. How much work did the drill do?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.40 kg, 𝐶= 897 J/(kg · K), 𝛥𝑇= 5.0 K. Assume no heat flows in or out (𝑄= 0).
First law: 𝛥𝑈= 𝑄−𝑊<sub>𝑏𝑦𝑏𝑙𝑜𝑐𝑘</sub>. With 𝑄= 0, 𝛥𝑈= −𝑊<sub>𝑏𝑦𝑏𝑙𝑜𝑐𝑘</sub>= 𝑊<sub>𝑜𝑛𝑏𝑙𝑜𝑐𝑘</sub>, so the work done by the drill on the block equals the increase in thermal energy, 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇.

answer.html: 𝑊= 1.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> J done by the drill on the aluminum

check.html: About 1.8 kJ for a few degrees in a small block is reasonable; positive because the drill adds energy.

items.title: 26, Dropping a bag of lead shot

question.html: How many drops of a 0.50 kg bag from 1.5 m heat the lead shot by 1.0°C?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.50 kg, ℎ= 1.5 m, 𝐶<sub>𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑑</sub>= 130 J/(kg · K), 𝛥𝑇= 1.0 K, 𝑔= 9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>. Find the number of drops 𝑛.
Each drop converts 𝑚𝑔ℎ of gravitational potential energy to thermal energy when the bag hits. Needed thermal energy is 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇.
The mass cancels. A whole number of drops is needed, so round up.

answer.html: About 9 drops (𝑛= 8.8)

check.html: Each drop supplies 𝑚𝑔ℎ= 7.4 J, and 1.0 K needs 65 J, so 65 / 7.4 ≈9.

items.title: 27, Stirring tea

question.html: Each stir does 0.050 J. How many stirs heat 0.15 kg of tea by 2.0°C?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.15 kg, 𝐶= 4180 J/(kg · K) (tea is mostly water), 𝛥𝑇= 2.0 K, 𝑊<sub>𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ</sub>= 0.050 J.
Work done on the tea becomes thermal energy: 𝑛𝑊<sub>𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ</sub>= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇.

answer.html: About 2.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> stirs (25,000)

check.html: A huge number, which is why stirring tea never noticeably warms it.

items.title: 28 (Challenge), Expansion valve doing work on 100 g of water

question.html: All work converts 100 g of water at 90°C into water vapor at 110°C, in an isolated system.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.100 kg, 𝐶<sub>𝑤𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟</sub>= 4180, 𝐶<sub>𝑣𝑎𝑝𝑜𝑟</sub>= 2020, 𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup>. 𝑄= 0 (isolated).
First law with 𝑄= 0: 𝛥𝑈= −𝑊<sub>𝑏𝑦𝑤𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑟</sub>, so the work done on the water equals its increase in thermal energy. Compute that increase as three steps: warm to 100°C, vaporize, warm vapor to 110°C.

answer.html: 𝑊≈2.3 × 10<sup>5</sup> J (2.32 × 10⁵ J) done on the water

check.html: Vaporization makes up 97% of the total, so the result is close to 𝑚𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 2.26 × 10<sup>5</sup> J.

items.title: Get It? (energy converted to a less useful form)

body.html: Energy is conserved but spreads out as thermal energy, which is hard to reuse.
A light bulb turns electrical energy mostly into thermal energy in the room; braking a car turns kinetic energy into thermal energy in the brakes and air; a phone charger warms up while charging.

answer.html: Example: braking a car turns its kinetic energy into thermal energy in the brake pads and air, which spreads out and cannot be used to move the car again.

check.html: In each example the final thermal energy is spread over many particles at a slightly higher temperature.

items.title: Get It? (pizza as an uncontrolled system)

body.html: An uncontrolled system has no outside agent keeping energy concentrated; energy follows the second law.

Nothing keeps the pizza hot: it sits freely in the room. Its particles have a higher average kinetic energy than the air's, so collisions at the surface pass energy to the air. This continues until the pizza and air have the same average kinetic energy, so the thermal energy ends up spread more evenly.

answer.html: No heater or insulation controls the pizza, so thermal energy spontaneously flows from the hot pizza to the cooler air until both are at the same temperature, which is a more uniform distribution of energy.

check.html: The air gets warmer by a tiny amount because it is so massive.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Systems and System Models, a system around the pizza (Figure 20)

body.html: A system model names what is included, where the boundary is, and what crosses it.

Choose the system as the pizza (the slice on its plate). The boundary is the surface of the pizza. Input: essentially none once it is out of the oven (before that, thermal energy from the oven). Outputs: thermal energy leaving through the boundary by conduction to the plate and air, convection by air currents, and radiation (infrared), plus a little energy carried off by evaporating water vapor.

answer.html: System: the pizza. Boundary: its outer surface. Input: none after leaving the oven. Outputs: thermal energy lost by conduction, convection, radiation and evaporation to the plate and air until equilibrium with the room.

check.html: If you widen the system to include the pizza and the room, the energy transfers become internal and total energy is constant.

items.title: Get It? (second law with entropy)

body.html: Entropy measures energy dispersal.
In natural (spontaneous) processes energy disperses, so entropy does not decrease.

answer.html: Natural processes go in the direction that keeps or increases the total entropy of the universe; entropy never decreases on its own unless work is done by an outside agent.

check.html: Hot soup spreads its energy to the room (entropy up) and never spontaneously refreezes.

answer.html: 1: 15 J/K; 2: 12 J/K; 3: 0.48 J/K; 4: 1.2 × 10<sup>3</sup> J/K. Why they differ: (1) vs (2): same heat, but the same energy added to a hotter object raises entropy less (smaller 1 / 𝑇). (1) vs (3): water has a much larger specific heat than lead, so the same temperature change needs far more heat, and so more entropy. (4): melting needs much more heat than a 1 K rise, at the same temperature, so the entropy increase is by far the largest (the particles gain many new ways to move).

check.html: All 𝛥𝑆 values are positive because energy was added to each system, and units are J/K.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Lesson 2 Problem 29, Heat engine: energy transformations and entropy

body.html: A heat engine takes in heat 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub> from a hot source, converts part to work 𝑊, and expels waste heat 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> to a cold sink: 𝑊= 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub>−𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> (since 𝛥𝑈= 0 over a cycle).

Thermal energy moves from the high-temperature source (such as burning fuel) into the engine, where part is transformed into mechanical energy (work), and the rest is transferred as waste heat to the cooler surroundings (exhaust, radiator). The waste heat disperses thermal energy into the large, cooler surroundings, so energy is spread out more than before, which is an increase in entropy; no engine can avoid this.

answer.html: Heat 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub> flows from a hot source into the engine; part becomes work 𝑊 and the rest leaves as waste heat 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> to a cold sink (𝑊= 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub>−𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub>). Operating the engine increases entropy because the waste heat spreads thermal energy into the surroundings.

check.html: Energy in equals work out plus waste heat, so the first law holds.

items.title: 30, Steam radiators

body.html: Condensation releases the heat of vaporization: 𝑄= −𝑚𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub> (the vapor loses 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg).

Steam reaches the cooler radiator and condenses to liquid water. The energy that was absorbed when the water vaporized is given back, a large amount per kilogram. This energy is conducted through the radiator metal to the room air, and convection circulates the warm air around the room.

answer.html: As the vapor condenses in the radiator it releases its heat of vaporization (about 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J per kg), which passes through the metal and warms the room air.

check.html: The sign of 𝑄 for the steam is negative (it loses energy) and positive for the room.

items.title: 31, Ice at −20.0°C to water at 10.0°C

body.html: Warm the ice to 0°C, melt it, then warm the water to 10.0°C.

check.html: Melting is the largest part, as in the other ice problems.

items.title: 32, Heating and vaporizing mercury

body.html: Warm the liquid to its boiling point, then vaporize it at constant temperature.

check.html: Vaporization is about 86% of the total.

items.title: 33, Hammer smashing lead against a rock

question.html: A 320 kg hammer at 5.0 m/s smashes a 3.0 kg lead block against a rock; the lead warms by 5.0°C. Explain how.

body.html: Mechanical energy is converted into thermal energy in an inelastic collision (work done on the lead).
The hammer's kinetic energy is
The lead's thermal energy rises by
so about half the hammer's energy ended up in the lead; the rest went into the rock, hammer and surroundings as thermal energy and sound.

answer.html: When the hammer stops, its kinetic energy (4.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> J) is converted by the collision into thermal energy of the lead, rock, hammer and air. About 2.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> J of it warmed the lead by 5.0°C ; energy is conserved overall.

check.html: The lead's 1.95 × 10<sup>3</sup> J is less than the hammer's 4.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> J, as required.

items.title: 34, Joule's waterfall

body.html: Falling water loses gravitational potential energy; when it hits the bottom and churns, its kinetic energy becomes thermal energy.
Energy is conserved: the mechanical energy lost by the water appears as thermal energy, so the water at the bottom should be slightly warmer.

answer.html: Joule expected the water at the bottom to be warmer, because the potential energy the water loses in falling (𝑚𝑔ℎ) is converted into thermal energy when it crashes into the pool.

check.html: This is the first law applied to mechanical energy (work equals heat equivalent).

items.title: 35, Temperature difference for the waterfall (Figure 22)

question.html: The waterfall in Figure 22 drops 125.0 m.

body.html: ℎ= 125.0 m, 𝑔= 9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 𝐶= 4180 J/(kg · K). Find 𝛥𝑇.
All potential energy becomes thermal energy: 𝑚𝑔ℎ= 𝑚𝐶𝛥𝑇. The mass cancels.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑇= 0.293 K (0.293°C warmer at the bottom)

check.html: A fraction of a degree is why Joule needed a very sensitive thermometer.

items.title: 36, Entropy and heating a home with natural gas

body.html: Entropy measures energy dispersal; it increases when energy spreads out.

Burning gas converts the concentrated chemical energy in the fuel into thermal energy of the combustion gases, then spreads it into the air in the house (and through the walls to the outdoors). The same energy is now spread over many more particles at a low temperature, so it is much less available to do useful work.

answer.html: Burning natural gas takes energy that was concentrated in chemical bonds and disperses it as thermal energy among a huge number of air molecules (and out to the surroundings). Energy is more spread out, so entropy increases.

check.html: The total energy is conserved, but it can no longer be easily gathered back, as the book says.

items.title: 37 (Critical Thinking), Misters at amusement parks

body.html: Evaporation needs the heat of vaporization (𝐻<sub>𝑣</sub>= 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J/kg for water).
Droplets of water evaporate quickly in the warm air. The energy to turn liquid to vapor comes from the surrounding air (and from your skin), so the air loses thermal energy and its temperature drops.

answer.html: As the fine mist evaporates it absorbs a large amount of thermal energy (the heat of vaporization) from the surrounding air, which cools the air.

check.html: Same reason sweat cools you.

items.title: 3D Thinking, model the combustion cycle of a gasoline or diesel engine

body.html: A four-stroke engine cycle (intake, compression, power, exhaust) is a heat engine: 𝑊= 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub>−𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub>.

A simple 2D model, drawn as four panels of a piston in a cylinder: Stroke Piston What happens (gasoline) What happens (diesel) 1. Intake moves down fuel-air mixture drawn in air only drawn in 2. Compression moves up mixture compressed air compressed much more; it gets hot 3. Power pushed down spark ignites mixture; gas expands, doing work fuel sprayed in; it ignites from the heat of compression 4. Exhaust moves up exhaust (waste heat) pushed out exhaust pushed out

answer.html: This is a hands-on model project, so no unique numerical answer exists. A correct model shows the four strokes above, labels 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub> (combustion heat in), 𝑊 (work to the crankshaft) and 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> (exhaust and radiator waste heat), and notes the diesel engine's higher compression, which allows no spark plug and gives higher efficiency.

check.html: Every model should show that 𝑊= 𝑄<sub>𝐻</sub>−𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub> with 𝑄<sub>𝐶</sub>> 0.
